sentences.text: This animal was a herbivore that moved on two legs but could also walk on four legs when needed.
The holotype specimen, which serves as the primary example for the species, was estimated to be about 6 meters long.
However, microscopic study of the bones showed the individual was not fully grown, suggesting the species could reach lengths of roughly 9 meters like its relatives.
Paleontologist Marc Boada found new fossil sites near the village of Abella de la Conca in the 1990s within the Talarn Formation.
Excavations at the Sant Romà d'Abella locality in the Tremp Formation of Catalonia began in the spring of 1985.
The first remains found at Sant Romà d'Abella were originally thought to belong to the genus Rhabdodon before being recognized as a new taxon.
Pararhabdodon was among the final non-bird dinosaurs to disappear during the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event.
The genus was named by Casanovas-Cladellas, Santafé-Llopis, and Isidro-Llorens in 1993.
The name means "near fluted tooth" and refers to a lambeosaurine hadrosaurid from the Maastrichtian of Spain, identified as the first member of its subfamily on the continent in 1999.
Later fossil material revealed that the animal was a hadrosaur rather than a primitive iguanodontian, leading researchers to reclassify it based on new cranial and jaw elements.
Pararhabdodon lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, between 67 and 66 million years ago, in what is now Europe.
A 2019 paper questioned whether specimen MCD 4919 truly belonged to Pararhabdodon isonensis because its ectopterygoid shelf differed from the holotype.
In 2001, Jason Head challenged the idea that Pararhabdodon was the first known European lambeosaurine.
